hints: Find the black piece that attacks the knight, and the line it uses.
The knight must leave the d-file. List the squares a knight can jump to from d4.
One of those squares is next to a black pawn. Check each landing square for an attacker.
items.explain: The rook attacks along the d-file, so any jump takes the knight off the file. The squares b3, b5, c2, c6, e2, f3 and f5 are all safe. The square e6 is not: the pawn on f7 would take the knight there.

feedback_by_move.d4e6: The knight lands on e6, a square the black pawn on f7 attacks, and nothing defends it there. It is taken for nothing.

items.prompt: Black to move. The white rook on c1 attacks your bishop on c5, and nothing defends it. Answer with a counterattack: attack a white piece worth more than the bishop.

claims.statement: The bishop on c5 is attacked and nothing defends it; no other piece of that side is loose.
The rook on c1 is the only white piece that attacks c5.
After Rd8 the rook attacks the white queen on d1.
After Rd8 the engine line does not lose material.
Taking the pawn on a2 instead leaves Black behind in the engine line.
After Rfd8 the rook attacks the white queen on d1.
After Rfd8 the engine line does not lose material.

hints: Which white piece is worth more than a bishop, and which of your pieces could attack it?
Your rook on a8 can move along the back row. Look for a square on the d-file.
If the rook goes to the d-file, it attacks the queen on d1. Which square is that?
items.explain: Either rook goes to d8 and attacks the queen, worth nine against the bishop's three. If White takes the bishop, Black takes the queen. White has to deal with the queen first, and the bishop gets time to be defended.

feedback_by_move.a8a2: That wins a pawn, but a pawn is worth less than the bishop. After the white rook takes the bishop, Black is behind. A counterattack must threaten more than you stand to lose.

hints: Two of your pieces are attacked. Which one is defended already, and by whom?
If the knight leaves, what happens to the bishop on c7?
The knight should stay. Find a queen move that adds a defender to the knight.
items.explain: The knight is the only defender of the bishop, so moving it would leave the bishop loose. The queen can instead defend the knight, and the knight stays where it guards the bishop. Qd8, Qa8, Qe5 and Qb5 all do that.

feedback_by_move.d5f4: The knight moves away and stops guarding the bishop on c7. The white rook then takes the bishop. Check what a moving piece was guarding.

items.prompt: Black to move. The white rook on c1 attacks your rook on c8 along the open file. Black plays Bc7. Which of the five answers is that?

claims.statement: The black rook on c8 is attacked and nothing defends it.
Bc7 is a legal move.
After Bc7 no white piece attacks the rook on c8.
After Bc7 the white rook attacks the bishop on c7.

hints: Where does the bishop stand compared with the two rooks?
Does the attacked rook move, or does something else change?
A piece standing between the attacker and its target is a block.
items.explain: The bishop stands on the line between the two rooks, so the white rook no longer attacks the rook on c8. That is a block. The attacked piece did not move, nothing new defends it, and nothing was captured.

claims.statement: The knight on d5 is attacked and nothing defends it.

hints: Did the attacked knight move?
After the move, can a black piece capture back on d5?
A new friend guards the knight from behind, so a capture could be answered.
items.explain: The knight stays on d5, and the rook now guards it along the d-file. If White takes the knight, Black takes back, and White has given a rook for a knight. That is a defence.

hints: Find the attacked piece, and look at what kind of piece attacks it.
A pawn is worth less than a bishop. Would a defender stop it?
Defending fails against a cheaper attacker, and the pawn on f4 is defended. Move the bishop to a safe square.
items.explain: The pawn on f4 attacks the bishop. A defender would not help, because the pawn takes the bishop and you take only a pawn back. Taking the pawn fails too, since the pawn on g5 defends it. The bishop has to move, and Bc5, Bd4, Bd2 and Bc1 do that safely.

feedback_by_move.e3f4: The pawn on f4 is defended by the pawn on g5, so taking it gives a bishop for a pawn.
feedback_by_move.a1e1: Defending does not help against a cheaper attacker. The pawn takes the bishop and you only get a pawn back.
